stories.primary_headline: Karnataka land reclaimed on paper, encroached again in reality: PAC

primary_source.headline: Karnataka land reclaimed on paper, encroached again in reality: PAC
primary_source.content: Bengaluru: Government lands remained under encroachment despite official claims of eviction, with the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) questioning whether authorities have actually cleared the parcels they reported as freed.Karnataka has a total of 62.56 lakh acres of government land.&nbsp;According to the latest PAC report, accessed by DH, over 12 lakh acres of government land across Karnataka are under encroachment.Provide fresh crop loans to farmers: R V Deshpande to Karnataka govtRevenue officials told the PAC that 2.68 lakh acres had been cleared of encroachments. The PAC inspected 43 such cases where authorities said the encroached land was recovered. The legislature committee, however, found that the usurpers were back in 22 cases, covering 219.14 acres of land.&nbsp;"If inspections are held across the state, it is possible that we will find more such cases where encroachments remain despite evictions," the PAC, headed by senior BJP lawmaker Araga Jnanendra wrote in its August 24 report.&nbsp;Citing the example of the Bengaluru Urban district, the PAC found that out of 31,050 acres of “valuable” land cleared of encroachments, only 1.5% had been “secured” by way of fencing and signage. In Bengaluru, like in other places, the PAC team found that the usurpers were back even after authorities claimed to have "recovered" the encroached land.&nbsp;The PAC frowned that encroachments were not cleared despite deputy commissioners facilitating evictions. "This has allowed encroachers to keep possession of government land," the report stated.In its report, the PAC also reviewed the functioning of the Karnataka Public Lands Corporation, established by the government for "conservation and better management" of government lands. The PAC stated that this government body is short-staffed and does not possess any special powers to fight encroachment of government land.&nbsp;The PAC further pulled up authorities for granting 89.31 acres of encroached government land to encroachers themselves. It cited two examples: two acres of Talkadu Jaladhama Resort (Mysuru) and 77.19 acres of the Eagleton resort in Ramanagara. "The PAC is of the opinion that granting encroached land to encroachers will only incentivize private individuals or organisations to usurp," the report stated.&nbsp;Karnataka sends drought memo to Centre, seeks Rs 20k crore under NDRFSkilled attorneysThe report asked the government to appoint skilled attorneys to fight its cases before courts of law.&nbsp;The Karnataka Land Grabbing Prohibition Special Court started functioning from August 2016. Up to April this year, the special court has disposed of 20,378 cases and 5,274 are pending. "The government has lost land due to inefficient and untimely handling of cases," the report stated.

stories.primary_headline: Bengaluru parks score low on accessibility: The topography of failing its citizens

primary_source.headline: Bengaluru parks score low on accessibility: The topography of failing its citizens
primary_source.content: Padmavathi Janardhanan would carry her son over the gates of public parks in and around Thippasandra until he was 15. Her son, now 46, has cerebral palsy and is a wheelchair user. “Once he got older, it became difficult and we stopped going to parks altogether,” she shares. Most park entrances in the neighbourhood did not have ramps and the gates would obstruct wheelchair entry. Years later, she believes that the issue of accessibility remains.A recent study of 120 parks across the city by think tank Pacta revealed that only 34.8% of them had barrier-free entrance for wheelchair users. “Our focus was heavily on whether they could play with and use the equipment. We also looked at the presence of lights, ramps, the height of benches, and the ability for a wheelchair to be stationed near a play area, among other things,” says Nivedita Krishna, founder, Pacta. She notes that while play equipment in these parks is mostly usable across ability levels, obstructions to entry was a common observation.&nbsp;Ranga Shankara theatre fest in Bengaluru spotlights belongingGround realityFor Yogitha Jagadeesh, whose son is diagnosed with global developmental delay and struggles to walk without some support, the unavailability of support is a challenge. “The washrooms don’t usually have additional safety rods, making them difficult to access,” she shares. As an alternative, Yogitha now settles for the playtime that her son gets during therapy sessions, and within the facilities at their gated society.Padma B Udaya Kumar’s 28-year-old daughter, who has cerebral palsy, finds it difficult to enter a public park near their home in Rajajinagar. “Though the park is beautiful, getting in is a challenge because there is no ramp,” says Padma. Their driver and the park’s security guard help lift her beyond the gate.Shakeeb Khan’s autistic son got lost in a crowded park owing to his tendency to explore and wander by himself. “The security guard finally helped find him, but it was challenging as his son is non verbal. An announcement system will be helpful,” he says. Having sensory elements like play items with varied textures and a clean water body would also make a difference for his child. “It is important that there are no exits on a main road or roads with heavy vehicular movement,” he adds.&nbsp;Balraj C, who is visually impaired, recommends installing signages with Braille and tactile maps for easier navigation. “I would want to move around parks independently. Not a lot of people are patient enough to offer help,” he says. Only 10.6% of parks from Pacta’s study had a map. Ashmira Hamirani, who is visually impaired and works with the Association of People with Disability (APD), says attitudes matter too. “Attitudinal openness is extremely important,” she says, adding that dogs, crowds and staff who haven’t been sensitised all make a park harder to use. She suggests ramps, step-free entrances, tactile paths, and training for security and maintenance staff.Creating better spacesShantesh Kelvekar, a landscape urbanist, points out that free mobility is often kept in mind during the design process, but it does not quite take shape when it comes to implementation. “Our drawings are not read well enough, diluting the accessibility aspect,” he says. Implementation engineers often interpret drawings without proper dialogue with designers and also tend to dismiss certain features as “non practical.” “Spaces are more sensitively designed when they are part of flagship projects. That sensitivity needs to trickle down to public spaces,” he adds. Besides ramps and well-positioned washrooms, he recommends colour-coded signages, lighting, and appropriate textures.&nbsp;Nivedita shares that volunteers were encouraged to locate persons with disabilities in the parks they surveyed. However, they could spot persons with visible disabilities. "We also thought about disabled caregivers. One of the visually-impaired people we consulted said that a park could become a place of stress," she says.&nbsp; The unpredictability of the experience also emerged as a common point. "A hose in the pathway may not make a difference to someone without a disability. But such small things can affect the experience for persons with disability," she adds.&nbsp;Bengaluru North Corporation Commissioner P Sunil Kumar says up to Rs 60 lakh of this year’s Rs 37-crore maintenance budget can go towards disability-friendly infrastructure in at least 15 parks in north Bengaluru. “Another Rs 4.5 crore from the welfare fund could pay for accessibility features in a couple of more parks. Work should start in a few months,” he says. The Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) is also looking to partner with NGOs to effectively solve accessibility issues.Designing accessibilityRampMyCity, a physical accessibility start up, built two accessible washrooms at Lalbagh last year and is working on four parks in collaboration with the Bengaluru South Corporation. They aim to incorporate reserved parking, tactile maps, and special swings and make washrooms accessible.Abhishek Thomas Robinson from the Association of People with Disability shares that a pilot at Richards Park in Lingarajapuram aims for inclusion, not only access: seating where wheelchair users sit beside family, a sensory area, and usable exercise equipment. It awaits budget approval and is slated for completion in February. “A lot of park entrances also have bars placed a foot apart from one another. Wheelchair users need a 4-feet space at least to enter,” he notes.

stories.primary_headline: US official: Russia's stalker satellite sure looks like an orbital weapon

primary_source.headline: US official: Russia's stalker satellite sure looks like an orbital weapon
primary_source.content:
Four years ago, a senior official in Russia's foreign ministry painted a bullseye on commercial satellite networks that assist Ukraine in its fight against invading Russian military forces.
On Wednesday, several days after a Russian military spacecraft moved within striking distance of one of those commercial satellites, the same Russian diplomat assured the world there's no reason to worry.
There's a sharp incongruity in those statements from Konstantin Vorontsov, deputy head of Russia's delegation to the United Nations. Vorontsov's comments Wednesday in the UN General Assembly's First Committee came moments after a US official called attention to recent maneuvers by Kosmos 2612, a Russian military craft that approached a US-registered commercial satellite some 340 miles (550 kilometers) above Earth.Read full article
Comments

stories.primary_headline: This emulator reimagines Nintendo’s Virtual Boy with a full color display

primary_source.headline: This emulator reimagines Nintendo’s Virtual Boy with a full color display
primary_source.content:
Last year, we reported on Red Viper, a Virtual Boy emulator that added a splash of Super Game Boy-style color to Nintendo's famously failed red-on-black "portable" 3D headset from the '90s. Now, a new emulation experiment, VBoy Color, has taken the concept to a higher level, using a tile-based palette system that allows for many more distinct colors in each individual Virtual Boy frame.
Rather than simply replacing the Virtual Boy's four shades of red with four different colors, VBoy Color's readme files explain how the emulator's game-specific Color Packs can assign a distinct four-color palette to each 8x8 tile in a Virtual Boy scene. That means the emulator can differentiate between green pipes, grey platforms, and red brick wall in Mario Clash, for instance, even though all those in-game objects share the same overlapping red hues in the original game.
The Game Boy Color-esque results feel like being transported into an alternate history where Nintendo invested in a full-color display rather than cheaper red LEDs for the Virtual Boy hardware. The increased contrast between differently colored elements is particularly welcome in games like Jack Bros. or Vertical Force, where the original red-on-red display often makes it hard to differentiate the player-character from busy red background elements.Read full article
Comments

Well, wonder no more – the answer is here, and it is The Audacity. It comes at you in hour-long episodes, which rush past at breakneck speed and leave you panting and deeply unsettled in their wake. Rather like modern life itself, of course, except for the relief available while the credits roll, before the next chunk of horrors arrives.The Audacity has a sprawling cast (especially in the opening episodes, which really are frenetic) but the figure around which most of the narratives move is Duncan Park (Billy Magnussen). He is the part-bullish, part-neurotic and wholly unbearable CEO of Hypergnosis, a data brokerage company he founded with a friend, who has since been struck by tragedy. Continue reading...

primary_source.content:
Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power returns next month for its third season. Prime Video unveiled a teaser earlier this year at San Diego Comic-Con, but we haven't heard much about the new season otherwise. We now have the official full trailer, and it's jam-packed with a rising Sauron, who is intent on conquering Middle-Earth with his army of Orcs—with the fractured opposition of elves, dwarves, and men scrambling to figure out how best to stop him. We also meet the human men who will become the Ringwraiths; the showrunners have dubbed them the Nazgnagol ("Rings-servant").
(Some spoilers for the first two seasons below.)
Prime Video made a major investment in The Rings of Power when it acquired the rights to the source material from the Tolkien estate, even committing to multiple seasons upfront. stories.primary_headline: Forget "Malaise 2.0," GM says it's still all-in on EVs and autonomy

primary_source.headline: Forget "Malaise 2.0," GM says it's still all-in on EVs and autonomy
primary_source.content:
GM provided flights from Detroit to New York and accommodation so Ars could attend the GM Future event. Ars does not accept paid editorial content.
It’s easy to criticize US automakers and their tepid approach to electric vehicles under the current administration and the expiration of the EV tax credit. It’s also easy to look at the rest of the world's embrace of EVs and wonder if the US is entering a “Malaise 2.0” era. Which is why GM wants the world to know that it is still focused on its end goals of electrification, autonomy, and improving vehicle quality while reducing development time.
At this year’s GM Forward event, company executives announced that its hands-off, eyes-off Super Cruise technology will expand across the lineup and be available on nearly every vehicle. This will include the pickup trucks and the crossovers, and not just the Escalade IQ that it was announced for last year.
Sterling Anderson, GM’s head of product, said the company is testing this technology to the tune of 1 million miles (1.6 million km) a month in both the virtual and real world. The goal is that not only would the vehicle be able to take you places, but it could go and do things for you.Read full article

stories.primary_headline: 333 Tor exit nodes hijacked to intercept SSH traffic and retrieve plaintext email

primary_source.headline: 333 Tor exit nodes hijacked to intercept SSH traffic and retrieve plaintext email
primary_source.content:
Unknown hackers hijacked more than 300 Tor exit nodes and reconfigured them to favor unencrypted email traffic and redirect SSH connections through servers they controlled, a researcher reported Tuesday.
The hijacking began in late August, when, according to Tor volunteers, the attacker used a valid password that had been reused to gain access to a Tor management server. The attacker then installed Ebury, a backdoor written for Linux that was discovered 12 years ago.
Mysteries remain
Then the attacker connected from the management server to a second Tor server, called Switzerland2, through SSH, using an RSA key that, for unknown reasons, investigators couldn’t find among Switzerland2’s authorized keys. With administrative control of Switzerland2, the attackers installed Ebury there as well. Finally, the attacker reconfigured settings on two exit nodes that Switzerland2 hosted.Read full article
Comments

stories.primary_headline: UN says we're going to blow past 1.5º warming, offers a "now what?" answer

primary_source.headline: UN says we're going to blow past 1.5º warming, offers a "now what?" answer
primary_source.content:
In 2015, all but two countries agreed to make an effort to keep global temperatures from reaching 1.5° C above pre-industrial readings. Since then, most of the world has largely treated what they signed on to as aspirational, and one of the largest emitters (the US) has alternately withdrawn and recommitted to the agreement. Meanwhile, the planet has responded as expected to steadily rising carbon emissions and appears to be practically at the 1.5° limit.
On Wednesday, for the first time, the United Nations Environmental Programme (UNEP) acknowledged that reality and conceded that the goal of keeping warming below 1.5° was no longer a viable one. Instead, its new goalposts focus on keeping both how long we exceed that limit and how much we exceed it by, at a minimum. Doing that will require both dramatic emissions cuts now and the removal of hundreds of gigatonnes of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere before the century is out.
Bowing to the inevitable
Depending on which baseline you use to establish pre-industrial temperatures, as well as which reconstruction of global temperatures you rely on, the world has either gotten very close to, or already exceeded, the 1.5° milestone. The current El Niño event, which appears exceptionally strong, will almost certainly mean that we've gone over it no matter which records you choose.Read full article

stories.primary_headline: Nintendo Switch Sports Resort review – Wii Sports lives on in this effortlessly appealing collection of games

primary_source.headline: Nintendo Switch Sports Resort review – Wii Sports lives on in this effortlessly appealing collection of games
primary_source.content: Nintendo Switch 2; Nintendo/NintendoBringing a holiday vibe and a generous selection of sport-themed games, this is exactly what you want from a family video gameWhen the first Nintendo Switch Sports brought the effortless fun of Wii Sports back into my living room in 2022, I was frankly delighted. My small children discovered the pleasure of waving a controller around in enthusiastic imitation of a tennis player, and the surprising subtlety of virtual bowling, working out how to twist the wrist just right to guarantee a strike. I did not expect this game to become a family fixture for the next several years as my kids got older and climbed up the online ranks in all six of its sports (plus the two that were added as free updates). Switch Sports is so beloved in my household that the release of Switch Sports Resort this week is the most anticipated gaming event of the year. To be fair, my children are a bit young for Grand Theft Auto.Nintendo Switch Sports Resort brings three of the six sports back – tennis, bowling, and volleyball – alongside golf and basketball. Then there are seven entirely new sports: boxing, table tennis, archery, thumb wrestling, skateboarding, jetski, and piloting a little prop plane. They are all intuitive, easy to get the hang of on the first or second attempt – some have more legs than others, in the long run – and all of them, crucially, are a little bit silly. Thumb wrestling in particular is cheerfully absurd, giving your characters gigantic thumbs on hands the size of their heads. Continue reading...

stories.primary_headline: Basma and Temir Alcy: NAD review – skulking, sultry French-Moroccan crew evoke this shifting season

primary_source.headline: Basma and Temir Alcy: NAD review – skulking, sultry French-Moroccan crew evoke this shifting season
primary_source.content: (Stroom)Vocalist Basma and group Temir Alcy offer a dark and disorienting listen that contemplates loss and new beginnings, stoking a captivating sense of tensionThe new album from French-Moroccan vocalist Basma and Paris-based group Temir Alcy comes just in time for the changing of the clocks. It’s a dark and disorientating listen, exploring themes of loss and new beginnings over swampy, downtempo rhythms. The 11 tracks here linger somewhere between folk, shoegaze and ambient, with skulking percussion, droning passages and plucked strings soaked in reverb. Opening track Belati sets the tone with its spacious, shapeshifting composition, where ghostly drones and Basma’s layered calls give way to a sluggish beat. Most of the tracks follow a similar non-structure: amorphous but with an intermittent, sultry groove, like the winding bass on Khti Sarah, or the slow, swinging rhythm on Aji M3aya.Basma’s performance is always captivating. Singing in a mixture of Darija (vernacular Arabic) and French, she delivers poetic snapshots in sensory terms that chime with the shifting seasons: “shy light”, blowing wind and bonfires. On Rised, breathy fragments are looped and reversed into a dreamy haze, while her lilting chants on La Tourne have a hypnotic effect. On standout Al Atlal, which lumbers along like a haunted lullaby, she drifts between soft wails and stoic spoken word. Continue reading...

stories.primary_headline: Can AI really predict cancer survival better than a doctor? I have my doubts | Devi Sridhar

primary_source.headline: Can AI really predict cancer survival better than a doctor? I have my doubts | Devi Sridhar
primary_source.content: Take a selfie to see how healthy you are: the idea is enticing and this new research is promising. But so many factors have been ignoredThe idea that a single selfie could predict how long someone with cancer may live sounds like an incredible breakthrough. AI is getting better at spotting patterns in medical data, but can it be used to reliably predict what will happen to an individual patient? I asked a clinical colleague what she thought about the recent headlines. She found it an interesting development given that doctors have long used facial appearance to assess patient health. For example, she noted that they may write “appears stated age” or “appears older than stated age” as a proxy for general health.Now, researchers from Mass General Brigham, a healthcare institution in Massachusetts, have taken this idea a step further. They have developed an AI model trained on more than 40 million facial images – called FAHR-Face – to assess biological age and predict survival in cancer patients. For biological age, they developed FAHR-FaceAge, which estimates age from certain facial features such as the forehead, the wrinkles between the nose and mouth and the temples. For cancer survival, they developed FAHR-FaceSurvival, trained using almost 35,000 photos of cancer patients. This model focused more closely on the area below the eyes and the bridge of the nose – regions of the face “linked with dying”. Dr Raymond Mak, one of the study’s authors, noted that these parts of the face are the same as those referenced by Hippocrates in 400BC as signs of muscle wasting and mortality risk: “the nose sharp, the eyes sunken, the temples fallen in”.Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh Continue reading...

stories.primary_headline: Record growth, rising risks: What’s really driving India’s core industries? | The Hindu Editorial

primary_source.headline: Record growth, rising risks: What’s really driving India’s core industries? | The Hindu Editorial
primary_source.content:
India’s core industrial sectors recorded a series-high growth rate of 7.9% in September, driven by strong performances in coal, electricity, steel and refinery products.

While the data points to a welcome industrial uptick, concerns remain about how sustainable the momentum will be. Much of the growth appears linked to temporary factors such as increased power demand during the heat wave and higher refining activity driven by imported oil.

With global crude prices rising, foreign exchange pressures mounting and infrastructure spending continuing to shoulder much of the growth burden, economists are questioning whether the current surge can be sustained in the coming months.

stories.primary_headline: Indian student arrivals in US fall 39% in August amid tighter visa checks

primary_source.headline: Indian student arrivals in US fall 39% in August amid tighter visa checks
primary_source.content: The number of Indian students arriving in the United States on student visas fell 39 per cent in August 2026 compared with the same month last year, according to data from the US Commerce Department’s International Trade Administration (ITA). The decline comes amid stricter immigration checks and uncertainty over work opportunities after graduation.The US recorded 25,321 arrivals from India on F and M category visas in August, down from 41,540 in August 2025. This was the lowest August figure since 2020, when pandemic-related travel restrictions limited arrivals to 2,908, Hindustan Times reported.August is usually a peak month for international student arrivals ahead of the fall semester. The decline follows a 44.5 per cent drop in August 2025 and a 20.3 per cent fall in August 2024.Explained | US student visa rules change: Universities ask students to return before September 15; who all could be affected? Student arrivals remain below previous yearsThe decline was also recorded in June and July, when arrivals from India on student visas fell 17.3 per cent and 30.6 per cent, respectively, compared with the same months in 2025.Arrivals rose 5 per cent in September to 12,285, up from 11,700 a year earlier. However, this was still 37.5 per cent lower than the September 2024 figure.Between June and September 2026, the US recorded 53,714 arrivals from India on student-category visas. This was 28.2 per cent lower than the same period in 2025 and 59.7 per cent lower than in 2024.US may impose $70,000 OPT fee for F-1 visa holders: How Indian students could be affectedThe data count arrivals rather than individual students and include dependants travelling on F-2 and M-2 visas. They are based on travellers’ country of residence and do not show how many visas were issued, how many students enrolled or the reasons for the decline.Stricter screening and visa delaysThe decline comes as the administration of US President Donald Trump has tightened checks on student visa applicants.A study published in April by US education company Shorelight, using government data obtained through a Freedom of Information Act request, found that the refusal rate for F-1 student visa applications from India rose from 36 per cent in fiscal 2023 to 53 per cent in 2024 and 61 per cent in 2025.India’s Ministry of External Affairs also told the Rajya Sabha in April 2026 that the US issued 12,776 F-1 visas to Indian nationals in June and July 2025, down from 41,336 in the same period in 2024. The ministry cited expanded US screening and compliance measures as factors affecting visa issuance.Laid off on H-1B visa? America mulls scrapping 60-day window to find a new jobProposed OPT fees add to uncertaintyUncertainty over work opportunities after graduation is another concern for students planning to study in the US.On October 8, 2026, the US Department of Homeland Security proposed charging educational institutions $70,000 for a student’s first period of Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for each subsequent period. OPT allows eligible international students to work in jobs related to their field of study after completing their course.&nbsp;A separate rule that would replace the existing system, under which international students can remain in the US for the duration of their studies, with fixed admission periods was blocked by a federal court on September 14. The rule remains on hold while legal proceedings continue.

primary_source.headline: Rupee rises 3 paise to 94.78 against US dollar in early trade
primary_source.content: Mumbai: The rupee traded in a narrow range and edged up 3 paise to 94.78 against the US dollar in early trade on Friday amid elevated crude oil prices and foreign fund outflows.Forex traders said rupee is under pressure amid persistent macroeconomic headwinds, including global dollar strength and Brent crude prices hovering near $113 per barrel.At the interbank foreign exchange market, the rupee opened at 94.78, registering a gain of 3 paise over its previous close.Rupee slumps 44 paise to close at 94.82 against US dollarRupee falls 12 paise to 94.50 against US dollar in early tradeOn Thursday, the rupee closed at 94.81 against the American currency.Foreign investors turned cautious seeking safe-haven greenback assets amid elevated US Treasury yields,  said Anil Kumar Bhansali, Head of Treasury and Executive Director Finrex Treasury Advisors LLP.Meanwhile, the dollar index, which gauges the greenback's strength against a basket of six currencies, was trading at 101.64, higher by 0.04 per cent.Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, was trading higher by 0.42 per cent at $113.65 per barrel in futures tradeSensex rose 343.48 points to 73,592.87, while Nifty gained 41.65 points to 22,729.30.Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs) offloaded equities worth Rs 3,458.70 crore on a net basis on Thursday, according to exchange data.

stories.primary_headline: IMA Keralam backs move to expand SMA treatment, seeks affordable drugs

primary_source.headline: IMA Keralam backs move to expand SMA treatment, seeks affordable drugs
primary_source.content: Kozhikode, Keralam: The IMA Keralam has said it welcomes the state health department's efforts to expand treatment for children with Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA), stressing the need to ensure affordable medicines and uninterrupted care.The doctors' body said the availability of lower-cost drugs could help reduce the financial burden of treating the rare genetic disorder and enable more children to receive treatment.SMA affects muscle strength, mobility and breathing, while medicines such as risdiplam play a crucial role in managing the progression of the disease, IMA Keralam said in a statement.The statement comes amidst a controversy over the Keralam Health Department's distribution of low-cost, Indian-made medicines to children suffering from SMA, a rare genetic disorder.The association said reducing drug costs could improve the financial sustainability of rare disease treatment programmes and help the government extend treatment to more children.However, it stressed that the quality and safety of medicines must be ensured and that all necessary approvals and scientific standards should be followed.Sexual allegations put Kerala spas under scannerTreatment decisions, whether involving branded or lower-cost alternatives, should be based on scientific evidence and expert opinion, it said.Referring to concerns raised by some parents after receiving medicine labelled as a sample in connection with the new drug's distribution, the association said the health department should provide a clear explanation regarding the medicine's source, quality assurance and distribution.Transparent communication was essential to address parental concerns and maintain confidence in treatment, it said.The doctors' body said the safety of children, continuity of treatment and public health interests should take precedence over disputes between drug brands.IMA Kerala state president Dr M N Menon and state secretary Dr Roy R Chandran, in the statement, also said the association supported efforts to reduce the cost of rare disease treatment and expand access to more children.Ensuring quality medicines at affordable prices and uninterrupted treatment would provide the greatest relief to patients and their families, it added.A political row erupted in Keralam recently after Leader of the Opposition Pinarayi Vijayan, in a recent Facebook post,  expressed shock over reports that experimental drugs meant for clinical trials were being given to children suffering from SMA without their parents' consent. He had demanded strict action against those responsible.State Health Minister K Muraleedharan had, however, rejected the criticism and said low-cost Indian-made SMA medicines were being provided to children based on the recommendations of an expert committee that assessed the quality of the drugs.

stories.primary_headline: HeLa to a new world where progress in science matches dignity for patient

primary_source.headline: HeLa to a new world where progress in science matches dignity for patient
primary_source.content: The omission of Henrietta Lacks, who donated the immortal cells that have facilitated biomedical research, from scientific history is a rare wrong that has been righted, recently. Thanks to the battle her family fought, today, more regulations will govern ethical research.

sources.headline: HeLa to a new world where progress in science matches dignity for patient

brief_bullets: Henrietta Lacks, an African American woman whose cervical cancer cells were harvested without her knowledge in 1951, has finally received historical and institutional recognition following a relentless advocacy campaign by her descendants. The landmark settlement between the Lacks family and biotechnology giant Thermo Fisher Scientific rectifies decades of medical exploitation that birthed the immortal HeLa cell line, which fundamentally transformed global biomedical research, vaccine development, and oncology. This watershed moment highlights systemic historical injustices in medical ethics while catalyzing modern institutional reforms to ensure patient consent, transparency, and dignity govern contemporary scientific research and commercialization practices.
why_it_matters_bullets: This milestone reshapes bioethical standards by reinforcing patient consent requirements and corporate accountability in biomedical research.

sources.headline: How citizen science is tracking changes in shorelines around the world

brief_bullets: The global CoastSnap initiative leverages crowdsourced smartphone photography across more than two hundred international locations to monitor rapid shoreline changes driven by weather and environmental shifts. Initiated in Australia in 2017, the project utilizes standardized camera cradles and community participation to overcome the labor-intensive hurdles historically faced by coastal researchers. This collaborative model demonstrates how public engagement can effectively scale data collection for critical climate and geographic research.

stories.primary_headline: POCSO survivor cannot be denied compensation solely due to absence of injury marks: Allahabad HC

primary_source.headline: POCSO survivor cannot be denied compensation solely due to absence of injury marks: Allahabad HC
primary_source.content: Lucknow: The Allahabad High Court has ruled that a survivor of sexual assault under the POCSO Act cannot be denied compensation merely because the medical report does not record physical injuries.In the order issued Thursday, a division bench of Justice Shekhar B Saraf and Justice Amitabh Kumar Rai directed authorities to pay Rs 3 lakh to a minor under the Uttar Pradesh Rani Lakshmi Bai Mahila Samman Kosh scheme within 10 days of the production of a certified copy of the order.The court held that the district steering committee's decision to withhold compensation was contrary to law and the provisions of the scheme.Under the scheme, survivors of sexual assault under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act are entitled to compensation of Rs 3 lakh. Of this, Rs 1 lakh is payable within 15 days of the FIR, while the remaining Rs 2 lakh must be paid within a month of the chargesheet being filed.‘Workload no excuse’: Allahabad HC orders release of cybercrime accused over remand lapsesThe case relates to an FIR registered at Sarojini Nagar police station in Lucknow on December 7, 2022. A chargesheet in this connection was filed on January 13, 2023.The district committee had withheld compensation citing the absence of medical evidence supporting penetrative sexual assault. The state counsel defended the decision, arguing that the medical report did not record injuries indicating penetration.Rejecting the argument, the high court observed that physical injury is not a necessary condition for establishing penetrative sexual assault under Section 3 of the POCSO Act.The bench held that absence of injury marks cannot, by itself, negate an allegation of sexual assault. Once the FIR and chargesheet indicate an offence under Section 4 of the Act, compensation cannot be denied solely because the medical report does not record injuries.Describing the scheme as a beneficial measure intended to alleviate the trauma and suffering of victims, the court said its provisions must be interpreted liberally.

stories.primary_headline: Oura sues rival Ultrahuman again, threatening its U.S. smart ring comeback

primary_source.headline: Oura sues rival Ultrahuman again, threatening its U.S. smart ring comeback
primary_source.content: Smart ring maker Oura has sued Indian rival Ultrahuman again, seeking to block U.S. sales of its Ring Pro (pictured above) just months after the redesign helped the Bengaluru-based startup return to the American market following an import ban. The case is the latest in a string of patent disputes Oura has brought against competing smart-ring makers, including Samsung and RingConn. In a complaint filed Thursday in a federal court in Texas, Oura alleged that Ultrahuman’s Ring Pro infringes two of its patents covering the ring’s design and internal components, including its battery and sensors. Oura is seeking monetary damages and a permanent injunction that would stop Ultrahuman from selling the ring. “Ultrahuman has a history of copying Oura’s innovations, as demonstrated by the 2025 ITC ruling against the company,” an Oura spokesperson said in a statement to TechCrunch. “Ultrahuman introduced a redesigned ring but failed to address continued infringement of Oura’s patents, seeking instead to capitalize on our innovation and the market leadership we have built.” Oura argues that the Customs ruling covered only the patent involved in the earlier dispute, not the two patents cited in its latest lawsuit: D804,471 and 12,769,363. “To protect its patent rights, Oura is now forced to file this complaint of patent infringement,” the company said in its filing. One of those patents, 12,769,363, is also very new. It was issued to Oura on October 20, just two days before it filed the lawsuit. It covers a smart-ring design incorporating internal components such as a curved battery, circuit board, magnets, and sensors. Oura has also named Texas-based electronics manufacturer SVTronics as a defendant in the lawsuit. The complaint says SVTronics manufactures the Ring Pro at a facility in Plano, Texas, allegedly under Ultrahuman’s direction and control. It also alleges that both companies infringe Oura’s patents through the manufacture, importation, and sale of the device in the U.S.

stories.primary_headline: Last One Laughing: Halloween review – still a total treat, despite the new twist

primary_source.headline: Last One Laughing: Halloween review – still a total treat, despite the new twist
primary_source.content: No screaming is allowed in the spooky spin-off, but the stars are only in danger of cracking up over these golden comedy moments. Even Jack Dee looks delighted to be there!British comedy is a broad church united by a simple adage: less is more. The most acclaimed and beloved shows – Fawlty Towers, The Young Ones, Brass Eye, The Office – tend to be exceptionally short-running. Compared to the Americans, our series are brief anyway, but we also seem anxious to bow out well before a premise is squeezed dry. We don’t milk it, we don’t money-grub. In a weird way, comedy is viewed as a precious finite resource liable to become exhausted at any moment.Which is why I feel slightly sceptical about this Halloween special of Prime Video’s Last One Laughing, the reality gameshow that involves a group of comedians competing to see who can remain straight-faced for the longest. The enormous success of the first two series – incredible ratings, healthy media coverage, a pair of Baftas – was well deserved: the show produced some of the most hysterical TV comedy in recent memory. You can understand why the streamer would be keen to capitalise on the interest of the circa 6 million-strong fanbase with this four-part miniseries, which whittles down the usual 10 contestants to seven. But might this snacky stopgap dilute the precious joy of the yearly series proper? Continue reading...

primary_source.headline: ‘I struggle to see myself as someone special’: Sandra Hüller on being the star of four - or, possibly, five - of the year’s biggest films
primary_source.content: New film Fatherland took Sandra Hüller back to a divided Germany. She talks about damaged dreams, Hollywood feelgood and - just maybe - appearing in the new Marvel movieSandra Hüller is crying, and it feels very strange. A wildly gifted actor, she can convey every human emotion there is. On screen, though, she is most often asked to embody deep self-possession. Even doing karaoke, Hüller is in control. And in real life, life is good. Her 2026 will end with four high-profile movies this year alone. Two (Fatherland and Rose) are black-and-white arthouse films that centre on her brilliance, and though one of the others (Digger) is already a Hollywood cautionary tale, a second (Project Hail Mary) was a giant $684m hit. (There may also be a fifth movie, bigger still. We will come back to that.)And yet, dressed in film star black, she is in tears. “This is really hard for me,” she says. Continue reading...

stories.primary_headline: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend

primary_source.headline: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend
primary_source.content: Max Dowman may get a chance, Spurs need to find balance at Stamford Bridge and Axel Disasi must make amendsPremier League top scorersAfter seven games, Nottingham Forest’s record is eerily similar to last season: five points, five goals scored. A year ago Forest’s eighth game was a 3-0 home loss to Chelsea that marked the end for Ange Postecoglou, the second of four managers to occupy the dugout last term. There is no suggestion that Oliver Glasner is under similar scrutiny yet, but the Austrian needs to find solutions for the league’s lowest scorers. Morgan Gibbs-White is available after missing the narrow defeat by Arsenal, while Liam Delap may benefit from a return to familiar surroundings – 12 of his 14 career Premier League goals were scored for Ipswich, six of them at Portman Road. “What we need to improve is getting [Delap] into more positions where he can score,” Glasner said before Friday evening’s game. “He’s one of our best finishers.” Gary O’Neil also lacks a standout scorer, but he is squeezing goals out of his side. Eight different Ipswich players have scored in seven games; only Brighton and Brentford can better that total this season. stories.primary_headline: Comcast loses more customers, claims other ISPs' cheap prices are "irrational"

primary_source.headline: Comcast loses more customers, claims other ISPs' cheap prices are "irrational"
primary_source.content:
Comcast reportedly plans significant job cuts in its cable division as the firm continues to lose residential broadband and TV customers. Comcast lost 144,000 residential broadband customers in Q3 2026, up from a 91,000-customer loss in the same quarter a year ago, the company said in its earnings report today.
Comcast historically capitalized on a lack of competition for high-speed wired broadband. But now it faces stronger competition from fixed wireless providers and from fiber providers in parts of its cable territory.
"Fixed wireless remains aggressive and continues to take share, while fiber construction remains elevated, with pockets of irrational pricing and promotional activity," Comcast co-CEO Mike Cavanagh said today in an earnings call.Read full article

stories.primary_headline: Disgraced eMudhra drops out of TLS business after using cert private key of 4

primary_source.headline: Disgraced eMudhra drops out of TLS business after using cert private key of 4
primary_source.content:
eMudhra, the certificate authority that issued eight intermediate TLS credentials so weak that anyone could mint certificates for any website or mail server—one had a private encryption key of just 4—said it’s getting out of the business.
V. Srinivasan, chairman of India-based eMudhra Limited, cited increasing costs and complexities of compliance requirements—paired with the business generating just 1 percent of its revenue. He also said that the emergence of organizations providing TLS certificates free of charge further reduced returns on investment when compared to other products and services the company offers.
Don't let the door hit you on the butt
“However, the level of social media amplification around this incident has brought scrutiny that is out of proportion to SSL/TLS’s place in our business,” the company continued in a Thursday post. “In view of this, after detailed deliberations our board has concluded that withdrawing from global SSL/TLS is the right decision for eMudhra and its shareholders.”Read full article

stories.primary_headline: Ink droplets in motion snag top prize in Nikon Small World contest

primary_source.headline: Ink droplets in motion snag top prize in Nikon Small World contest
primary_source.content:
A 25-year-old German experimental photographer has won the 2026 Nikon Small World photomicrography competition with a striking image of droplets of ink being deposited on paper by an inkjet printer. Ole Bielfeldt beat out 1,802 other entries hailing from 69 different countries.
Bielfeldt became interested in photomicrography during the COVID-19 lockdown after discovering an old microscope in his parents' attic. He figured out how to build an adaptor out of a tube and some wood to connect the microscope to his father's camera and taught himself the art through trial and error, building custom tools as needed. He documents how he captures transformative images of everyday objects with behind-the-scenes videos posted to macrofying, his photography and videography brand.
It was Bielfeldt's curiosity about the inner workings of inkjet printers that inspired his winning entry, but capturing the action of ink drops being deposited on paper was a challenge, given that the process happens so quickly. The droplets, for instance, moved faster than the camera's shutter speed. Bielfeldt's solution was to deconstruct the printer so that the paper moved under a stationary (rather than moving) printhead, and then take the image in a dark room, using a flash to serve as the shutter, thereby freezing the ink drops mid-air. There was no need for pricey equipment. Bielfeldt does not use AI in his images, preferring to rely on traditional techniques.Read full article

stories.primary_headline: Electric or gas? BMW goes both ways with new 2027 X5 and iX5.

primary_source.headline: Electric or gas? BMW goes both ways with new 2027 X5 and iX5.
primary_source.content:
BMW provided flights from Washington, DC, to Los Angeles and accommodation so Ars could drive the new X5 and iX5, as well as a refreshed i7 (which you can read about soon). Ars does not accept paid editorial content.
When we first drove BMW’s first Neue Klasse model, the iX3, it quickly revealed that BMW knows how to make a good electric vehicle. A clean-sheet design, it featured the automaker’s sixth-generation electric powertrain, a completely reimagined dashboard, and powerful computers to run the whole show. Now, much of that technology is being ported over to the larger X5 line.
But BMW knows not all its customers are ready to go electric, especially in the US, so it’s sticking with its powertrain-agnostic CLAR platform, as used in cars as diverse as the large 7 Series and the new gasoline 3 Series. Which means in addition to the all-electric iX5, there are also mild hybrid and plug-in hybrid X5s available, and in time, even a hydrogen-powered option. For now, as I’ll explain, I think the EV is the pick of the bunch.

      
      
        
    
    
      Get used to it, because this is what BMW SUV kidney grilles look like from now on.

              
          Credit:

          
          BMW

                  
          
  
      
    
      
      
      
        
    
    
      If you looked very carefully you'd see this was an iX5 because there's no exhausts. Of course, reading the badge is probably easier.

              
          Credit:

          
          BMW

                  
          
  
      
    
  
Pick your power
The most conventional option is the X5 40 xDrive, powered by a 3.0 L turbocharged inline six-cylinder engine that generates 394 hp (294 kW) and 428 lb-ft (580 Nm). The 48 V mild hybrid system can contribute a decent slug of torque (148 lb-ft/200 Nm) if necessary, and the engine operates under the Miller cycle for better efficiency, as well as featuring the usual BMW engine technology, like variable valve timing. Expect around 26 mpg (9 L/100 km) from this powertrain and a full-to-empty range of 569 miles (915 km).Read full article

stories.primary_headline: OpenAI makes its Jev competitor widely available as decision model competition heats up

primary_source.headline: OpenAI makes its Jev competitor widely available as decision model competition heats up
primary_source.content: Nikunj Handa, the product lead for OpenAI’s APIs, told TechCrunch that his colleagues saw Jev and said “wow, we we have like a million use cases for this.” Handa’s team sprinted to offer their own version: Rather than building a specifically calibrated decision model, the team took ChatGPT Luna and reconfigured it to speed up the inference and lower the cost. “The big unlock with Decisions API has been the speed, shrinking things from one to three seconds to 100, 120, 180 milliseconds,” Handa said. “In the future, we may sort of like have specific training to make our models like even better in these ways. But right now, it’s just plain old Luna that gets the job done.” Announced at the company’s developer day on September 29, the Decisions API became available to all customers on Thursday. OpenAI added new voice and visual modalities to the public version, and worked to ensure lower latency in regions around the world by targeting its inference resources geographically. In initial trials with customers like Box, Datadog, Ramp, and Speak, engineers used the API to replace OpenAI’s LLMs with higher throughput. Andrew Hsu, the CTO at Speak, which builds AI language tutors, said the Decisions API allowed the company to cut the time between actions from 1.4 seconds to .13 seconds. OpenAI also used the product to improve their Dots voice assistant’s responsiveness. Where OpenAI’s arguably more capable model may have an advantage is in multi-modality—for image classification, “Luna is extremely powerful and has been showing better calibrations,” Handa told TechCrunch, adding that OpenAI customers want the Decisions API to be more flexible about using images as outputs as well. Handa also saw further increases in speed enabling new use cases: “Can we get this to something like you know 60 milliseconds, and then you could imagine like an API like call like for every single frame in like a video?”

stories.primary_headline: Meta shocked by $25B fine after N.M. refused to join multistate settlement

primary_source.headline: Meta shocked by $25B fine after N.M. refused to join multistate settlement
primary_source.content:
Meta must pay $25 billion to New Mexico after a jury found the tech giant guilty of nearly 44 million violations of state consumer protection laws.
The largest fine to ever hit Meta came after New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez declined to join an $18 billion settlement Meta reached earlier this year with attorneys general in nearly all states.
In his opinion Wednesday, US district court judge Francis J. Mathew said there was no “bright line rule” for determining the appropriate penalty for Meta's repeated and willful deception of users since 2010 about their “control of data, third-party data misuse, misinformation, hate speech, and equal enforcement.”Read full article
Comments

stories.primary_headline: US-backed vaccine trial on babies canceled after international outcry

primary_source.headline: US-backed vaccine trial on babies canceled after international outcry
primary_source.content:
Government officials in Guinea-Bissau have formally rejected a clinical trial that would be run by Danish researchers and funded by the US to look for alleged nonspecific harms from the newborn dose of the hepatitis B vaccine. The vaccine dose is currently recommended globally for all newborns and has been used safely and effectively for decades.
In an email to Ars Technica, one of the trial's lead researchers, Christine Stabell Benn of Bandim Health Project and the University of Southern Denmark, said that Guinea-Bissau's Council of Ministers "formally reaffirmed its non-acceptance of the study on 16 October."
The revelation that the study was formally rejected last week comes after news on Monday that judicial police in Guinea-Bissau raided Bandim Health's offices and seized vaccines. Stabell Benn highlighted that the police search came after the trial was rejected.Read full article
Comments

stories.primary_headline: Glee’s pro-LGBTQ+ vision captured 2010s hope. Can a reboot handle Trump’s America? | Alim Kheraj

primary_source.headline: Glee’s pro-LGBTQ+ vision captured 2010s hope. Can a reboot handle Trump’s America? | Alim Kheraj
primary_source.content: The beloved high school TV show is returning in a different political climate. I’m skeptical that Ryan Murphy has the nuance this moment needsFor months, Ryan Murphy has been discussing Glee. In July, he expressed his love for the musical comedy drama he created. In September, he said that he had finished writing a pilot for a potential reboot, adding that he had reached out to some of the cast about a reunion. And now it is official: Disney+ and Hulu have commissioned a Glee revival.Glee, which ran for six seasons between 2009 and 2015, was a cultural juggernaut during its initial tenure. The show won six Emmys, four Golden Globes and made stars of actors including Lea Michele, Jonathan Groff, Chris Colfer, Darren Criss and the late Cory Monteith and Naya Rivera. Centred on the trials of New Directions, a scrappy show choir at the fictional McKinley high school in Ohio, the show became known for its peppy covers of show tunes, 80s power pop hits such as Journey’s Don’t Stop Believin’ (a Glee signature), 2010s chart-toppers and some truly baffling mashups (the amalgamation of Scissor Sisters’ Let’s Have a Kiki and Turkey Lurkey Time from Promises, Promises remains … a choice). primary_source.headline: Blockades, checkpoints and court action: fending off Brazil’s biofuel giants in the Amazon
primary_source.content: After decades of violent displacement and land theft, the country’s quilombola communities are fighting backFor most of his 39 years, Josias Dias dos Santos, known as Jota, has endured degrading cycles of displacement as a quilombola, a descendant of Black people once enslaved on Brazil’s sugar cane and coffee plantations. He says his and other quilombola families subsisting in the rainforests in Pará, northern Brazil, were first forced out of their settlements by violent loggers, then by ranchers and miners.Yet, they say the worst came with the arrival of the palm oil industry in what is now the country’s most deforested state. Palm oil companies producing biofuels and supplying global customers, subsidised by the federal government, have laid claim to ever larger tracts of traditional quilombola territory over the past two decades.
